title: Nets of 3-D Shapes
keyIdea: A net is a flat 2-D pattern that folds into a 3-D shape. The faces of the solid are drawn joined edge to edge so that when you fold along the edges, every face meets without overlapping. A cube net has 6 equal squares; only some arrangements of 6 squares fold into a cube. A cuboid net has 6 rectangles that match its faces. Checking that faces match, and that they do not pile on top of each other when folded, is how you test a net.

kid: A net is a flat drawing that folds up into a solid. Think of an open cardboard box flattened out.
A cube has 6 square faces. Its net is 6 squares joined edge to edge. When you fold them, they make the cube.
Not every pattern of 6 squares works. If two squares would land on the same face, or if a square sticks out where there is no room, it is not a net.
A cuboid is a stretched cube. Its net uses rectangles that match the front, side and top faces. Match the sizes before you fold.
adult: In the National Curriculum for England, Year 5 Geometry asks pupils to identify 3-D shapes, including cubes and other cuboids, from 2-D representations. Nets appear in Year 6 and KS3 as a standard way to link surface area to the faces of a prism. This lesson is about recognising and testing nets, not yet about calculating surface area.

A valid net places every face of the solid once, joined along edges that really meet on the solid, so that folding does not make two faces occupy the same place. There are 11 distinct nets of a cube. Crosses, zigzags and branched chains appear; a straight row of 6 squares never works, and a 2-by-3 rectangle of squares never works either.

Common mistakes: thinking any 6 squares make a cube net; forgetting to check that faces have matching edge lengths on a cuboid; counting tabs or flaps as faces; and confusing a net with an isometric drawing of the solid.
In the lab your child folds a cube net, rejects two false cube nets, builds a cuboid net from matching rectangles, and matches three nets to the solids they make.

familyTip: Open a clean cereal box carefully along the glued edges and flatten it. Count the faces and see how they join. Then try to sketch the net before you fold it back. Kitchen roll tubes are cylinders: their net is a rectangle plus two circles.

practice.prompt: How many faces does a cube have?
practice.hint: Count the sides of a dice.
practice.explain: A cube has 6 square faces: front, back, left, right, top and bottom.

choices: a flat pattern that folds into a 3-D shape
a drawing of a solid from an angle
practice.hint: Think of an opened cardboard box.
practice.explain: A net is the flat 2-D pattern of faces that folds into the solid.

practice.prompt: Which cannot be a cube net?
practice.hint: When you fold a long row, the ends meet in a problem.
practice.explain: A straight row of 6 folds into a tube with two faces left over that have nowhere to go. Crosses and many zigzags do work.

practice.prompt: A prism has {a} rectangular side faces and {b} end faces. How many faces in total?
practice.hint: Add the rectangular side faces to the two ends (or however many ends).
practice.explain: {a} rectangular faces + {b} ends = {=a+b} faces on the net and on the solid.

practice.prompt: A drawing shows {a} squares joined, which is {b} more than a cube needs. How many squares are on the drawing?
practice.hint: Start from a real cube net (6 squares) and add the extras you drew by mistake.
practice.explain: The drawing has {a} squares. A cube needs only 6, so this has {b} too many and is not a cube net.

pool.prompt: How many distinct nets does a cube have?
pool.hint: There are more than you might first think.
pool.explain: There are 11 distinct nets of a cube (counting rotations and reflections as the same).

pool.hint: Fold it in your head: faces crash.
pool.explain: Folding a 2-by-3 block makes faces overlap, so it is not a cube net.

pool.prompt: What is the net of a cylinder (roughly)?
choices: a rectangle with a circle at each end
pool.explain: The curved surface unwraps to a rectangle; the two ends are circles.

pool.prompt: Tabs on a cardboard net are for…
pool.explain: Tabs are for sticking. They are not faces of the solid, so do not count them in the net of faces.

pool.hint: Think of a tent shape. Count faces and check whether folding would overlap.
pool.explain: Two ends are triangles; three sides are rectangles (or parallelograms).

pool.prompt: A net shows {a} faces of a solid that has {b} faces in total. How many faces are missing from the net?
pool.hint: Subtract. Count faces and check whether folding would overlap.
pool.explain: {b} − {a} = {=b-a} faces are missing, so it is not a complete net.

pool.prompt: Lee draws 7 squares joined edge to edge and says it is a cube net. Is Lee right?
choices: No, a cube has only 6 faces
Yes, if one is a tab
pool.hint: Count the faces of a cube.
pool.explain: A cube has exactly 6 faces, so a net of 7 squares is not a cube net. A tab is not a face.

pool.prompt: On a cuboid net, two faces that share an edge on the solid must…
choices: share an edge in the net, or be joinable by folding
pool.explain: Faces that meet on the solid meet along an edge in the net or after a fold. Matching edge lengths matter on a cuboid.

pool.prompt: One net has {a} faces and another has {b}. How many faces across both nets?
pool.hint: Add the faces on the first net to the faces on the second.
